notes.html:
Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time

This section covers the network you rent: a VPC, its subnets, the gateways that let traffic out, and the rules that let traffic in. One idea runs through all of it: reachability and permission are separate systems, and only one of them is reversible. Route tables decide whether a packet can arrive. Security groups and NACLs decide whether it may. A meter decides what it costs. You can change routes and rules in an afternoon, but the address plan underneath them can't be changed without a rebuild.

Concept map

The address plan comes first because every later note routes, filters or bills traffic between addresses chosen there.

Green holds a CORE note, blue is SUPPORTING, yellow is BREADTH. 122–123 holds two CORE notes; 124–125 one CORE (124) and one SUPPORTING (125). Neighbours: CIDR arithmetic and NAT below this section, L4 vs L7 beside 132, and CNI plugins after it, where pods start spending VPC addresses.

Reading order:VPC mental modelsubnets and CIDR planningroute tablesIGW, NAT and egressSG vs NACLpeeringTransit Gatewayendpoints and PrivateLinkprivate DNScloud LBsthe billmulti-regionpostureVPN, Direct Connect, admin access

Route tables are read before egress (125 before 124) because "public subnet" is defined by a route.

  • Ten minutes before a tech discussion: redraw the three-tier, three-AZ VPC with its route tables; say "five reserved, /20 default, 100.64 for pods"; say "NAT: two meters, 55,000 per destination per IP"; walk the reach-it tree above.

headings.text: Operator access: bastion, client VPN, Session Manager

notes.html:
Two ways in from outside the VPC: networks reaching networks, and people reaching machines. Both land on the Transit Gateway or the route tables of the VPC they enter.

Site-to-site VPN vs Direct Connect

Stage: route · design time

Both join an office or data centre to a VPC. A site-to-site VPN is IPsec over the internet: up in minutes, cheap, encrypted, with internet jitter. Each AWS connection has two tunnels, and you need both for redundancy. Direct Connect (Azure ExpressRoute, GCP Cloud Interconnect) is a private circuit into a provider facility: steady latency, committed bandwidth and lower egress rates, but weeks of lead time. It isn't encrypted by default; add MACsec or IPsec over it. The usual shape: Direct Connect primary, VPN as backup on a different path, both into the hub. Plan non-overlapping CIDRs first.

Operator access: bastion, client VPN, Session Manager

Stage: secure · per connection

A bastion is a hardened host with a public IP you SSH through: an open inbound port, keys to rotate, a host to patch. A client VPN puts the laptop on the network, which is right when people need broad access to many resources. Session Manager reverses the direction: an agent on the instance dials out, so there's no inbound port, no public IP and no SSH key. IAM grants access, and CloudTrail plus session logs record it. It has displaced bastions for shell access; see posture.

notes.title: VPC — The Mental Model
notes.html:
References

AWS: Amazon VPC documentation · AWS: Understanding Amazon DNS · Google Cloud: VPC networks · Microsoft Learn: Virtual networks and virtual machines in Azure · AWS: VPC BPA basics

TL;DR

A VPC is a private L3 address space inside one cloud region. The provider's fabric does the routing, addressing and DNS on hardware you never see. Isolation is the default state: nothing reaches the internet, another VPC or your office until you attach a gateway and write a route. Every later note in this section answers one of two questions: how traffic leaves, and what is allowed back in.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:pick a CIDR (permanent)carve subnets per AZattach gatewayswrite routesattach security groupstraffic flows only where all of them agree

Recall

Prompt Answer
What layer is a VPC? L3: an isolated IP address space. Not a firewall, not a physical network.
Regional or global? AWS and Azure: regional, subnets zonal (AWS) or regional (Azure). GCP: the VPC is global, subnets regional.
Two VPCs, same CIDR: conflict? No, until you try to connect them. Peering and Transit Gateway refuse overlap.
What sits at base + 1 and base + 2? The VPC router (fabric, not a device) and the Amazon DNS resolver.
The one property you can't change later? The primary CIDR. Subnets too. Everything else is a config change.
Draw by hand: one VPC public subnet (ALB, NAT) → private subnet (app) → isolated subnet (DB, no default route); IGW at the edge; the route table decides each tier.

The idea

A team runs two clusters in two VPCs, both 10.0.0.0/16 because that was the console default. A year later the analytics VPC needs to read from production. The peering request fails with an overlap error, and the only fix is to rebuild one of them.

Nothing went wrong on day one: the VPCs were fully isolated and worked. The cost came due only when someone tried to connect them, because a VPC's isolation comes from the provider's overlay and not from anything you configured. Two identical address spaces live side by side happily until a route has to tell them apart.

The trade: a VPC gives you isolation for free and charges for every connection you add later, so the decisions that count are made before the first resource exists.

How it works

One VPC, three tiers in one AZ. No subnet has a "public" flag: the target of its default route decides the tier, and the internet gateway sits at the VPC edge.

Rule What actually happens
The overlay Each host encapsulates your packets and delivers them only to the destination's host. There is no broadcast domain: ARP spoofing and sniffing don't work, which is why traffic mirroring is a paid feature.
The router Every subnet's gateway at base + 1 is the fabric itself. Nothing to size, patch or lose, and nothing you can install in the path without a provider hook such as GWLB.
The resolver base + 2 (also 169.254.169.253) answers private zones, endpoint names and the internet. enableDnsSupport = false removes it.
The default No route, no path. Internet, peers, on-prem and managed services each need a gateway and a route, which route tables own.

Address demand is set by the workload, not by the server count:

demand ≈ instances + ENIs + LB nodes + endpoint ENIs + pods      ← with the AWS VPC CNI, every pod is a VPC IP
200 nodes × 30 pods = 6,000 addresses before anything else       ← why /16 stops being "obviously enough"

Evolution

Lineage:2006 EC2 on one shared flat networkAug 2009 Amazon VPC2013 new accounts get a default VPCNov 2024 VPC Block Public AccessMar 2026 new Azure VNets private by default
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): every cloud's compute lives in one.
  • Changed recently: account-wide guard rails. VPC Block Public Access can block internet-gateway traffic for a whole region, and Azure removed default outbound access from new VNets after 31 Mar 2026.
  • What won't change: isolation by overlay, so connecting networks is always an explicit product, never a firewall rule.

On the wire

Annotated Terraform for the VPC above, with the defaults that bite:

resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block           = "10.20.0.0/16"   # PERMANENT. From the org plan, never the 10.0.0.0/16 default.
  enable_dns_support   = true             # default true: turning it off kills the .2 resolver,
                                          # private hosted zones and every interface endpoint's DNS
  enable_dns_hostnames = true             # default FALSE for non-default VPCs: private zones
}                                         # and endpoint private DNS need it on

resource "aws_vpc_ipv4_cidr_block_association" "pods" {
  vpc_id     = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block = "100.64.0.0/16"            # secondary block for pods: added later, never resized
}

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026), not a cloud call: can two VPCs that each work alone be joined?

import ipaddress as ip
a, b = ip.ip_network("10.0.0.0/16"), ip.ip_network("10.0.128.0/17")
print(a.overlaps(b))           # the second team "only took half"
# look for: True, so no route table can send 10.0.200.5 to the right VPC
# naive belief predicts: False, because the two VPCs never conflicted while isolated

Run: True. 10.0.0.0/16 vs 10.1.0.0/16 prints False. Peering owns what happens next.

Measure it

  • See it: aws ec2 describe-subnets --query 'Subnets[].[SubnetId,AvailabilityZone,AvailableIpAddressCount]' shows free addresses per subnet; dig @10.20.0.2 internal.example from an instance proves the resolver.
  • In production: AvailableIpAddressCount per subnet with an alert at 20% left; cross-AZ bytes as a share of the bill; VPC flow-log REJECT counts by interface.
  • Bounded by: address exhaustion → a secondary CIDR (CIDR planning); accidental public exposure → VPC Block Public Access and no IGW route (posture).

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A VPC is a private L3 address space in one region, run by the provider's overlay. Isolation is the default: nothing gets in or out until you attach a gateway and write a route, so subnets, NAT, peering and endpoints are each an answer to "how does traffic leave and what may return". The primary CIDR can never change, so I plan addresses before drawing boxes.

Q · Mechanism — What is actually virtual about it? The addressing and routing; the packets are real. Each hypervisor maps your private IPs to physical hosts and encapsulates packets across the provider's fabric. So there's no broadcast domain to sniff, and the router at base + 1 is the fabric, not a box that can fail. The cost: you can't put anything in the path unless the provider sells a hook.

Q · Trade-off — One shared VPC or many small ones? One VPC per environment per region per account. Teams are split by security group and IAM inside it, and shared-VPC subnet sharing gives each account its own resources in one address space. More VPCs buy hard blast-radius boundaries but cost peering or hub attachments, per-VPC NAT and duplicated endpoints. Split for a compliance boundary, not for team count.

Q · Failure — What runs out first as a VPC grows? Addresses, and it's the only limit you can't raise. With pod-per-IP CNIs, a cluster drains one subnet in one AZ. Pods sit in ContainerCreating with "failed to assign an IP address" while other AZs have room, so it looks like a scheduling bug. Fix: a 100.64.0.0/10 secondary CIDR and prefix delegation. Route entries, security groups and ENIs are raisable quotas.

Q · Design — VPC topology for a multi-tenant AI product, three environments, two regions.

  • Address plan first: a /12 for the organisation, a /16 per region per environment, 100.64/10 for pods, nothing overlapping.
  • Per VPC: public subnets for load balancers, private for workloads and GPU nodes, isolated for data, each in three AZs.
  • Between VPCs: a Transit Gateway per region in a network account, the two regions peered, and egress through one inspection VPC that holds the hostname allow-list.
  • Watch first: free IPs per subnet, then cross-AZ bytes, then hub attachments against quota.

Compare

Concept AWS GCP Azure Why it matters
Network VPC, regional VPC, global VNet, regional cross-region on GCP needs no peering
Subnet one AZ one region one region AWS needs a subnet per AZ per tier
Instance firewall SG, stateful, on the ENI firewall rules, stateful, by tag or service account NSG, stateful, NIC or subnet AWS's SG-references-SG is identity-like
Subnet firewall NACL, stateless none NSG on subnet only AWS makes you write return rules
Transitive routing no; needs a hub yes inside one VPC no; needs a hub or vWAN non-transitivity drives most AWS topology work

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Reserved addresses per subnet 5 network, router, DNS, future, broadcast spec (as of Nov 2026): AWS subnets docs
VPC CIDR sizes /16 to /28 /28 leaves 11 usable spec (as of Nov 2026): AWS subnets docs
Resolver address base + 2, and 169.254.169.253 10.20.0.2 here spec (as of Nov 2026): AWS Amazon DNS
Pod addresses, 200 nodes × 30 pods 6,000 before nodes, ENIs and LBs derived

Pitfalls

  • "Public subnet means its instances have public IPs"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the console shows "auto-assign public IP" right on the subnet.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: public means the route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an IGW. A public IP behind a NAT route is unreachable; an IGW route without a public IP reaches nothing.
    ↳ Think instead: address and route are two facts; internet access needs both.
  • Not the same: VPC boundary vs security group
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both "isolate" workloads.
    ↳ Difference: a VPC boundary removes the route entirely; a security group filters traffic that is routable.
    ↳ Think instead: separate environments by VPC, teams by security group.
  • Don't use the default VPC for real work.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it already exists in every region and launches just work.
    ↳ What goes wrong: its subnets are all public and its 172.31.0.0/16 is every other account's too.
    ↳ Do instead: build an addressed VPC from the plan; delete or ignore the default.
  • "Two VPCs with the same CIDR will conflict"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: on-prem, duplicate subnets on one network break each other at once.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the overlay keeps their packets apart, so both work indefinitely; the conflict appears only when you peer or attach them.
    ↳ Think instead: plan for connections you haven't designed yet, because that is the only time overlap hurts.
  • "A /16 is obviously enough"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: 65,536 addresses dwarf any server count.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: pods, ENIs, endpoints and five reserved per subnet spend it, and exhaustion is per subnet, per AZ.
    ↳ Think instead: count pods, then put them on a 100.64 secondary block.
  • Shelf life: the overlay, isolation by default and immutable CIDRs are durable; guard rails such as Block Public Access and Azure's outbound defaults keep moving.

Connections

Path:routing basicsVPC mental modelsubnets and CIDR planningroute tables
  • Builds on private vs public IP: a VPC is built from RFC 1918 space.
  • Owned elsewhere: CIDR planning owns sizing; SG vs NACL owns filtering.
  • Breaks when combined with pod-per-IP CNIs: address demand jumps tenfold.
  • Bounded by the bill: every boundary crossing is metered.

notes.title: Subnets, AZs & CIDR Planning — The One Irreversible Decision
notes.html:
References

AWS: Subnets for your VPC · AWS: Subnet route tables · Google Cloud: Subnets · Google Cloud: Best practices for VPC design · 📜 RFC 6598: IANA-reserved IPv4 prefix for shared address space

TL;DR

On AWS a subnet lives in exactly one AZ, so three tiers across three AZs is nine subnets. Each loses five reserved addresses, and neither a subnet nor the VPC's primary CIDR can ever be resized. Two rules follow. Size big, because over-allocating costs nothing and under-allocating means a rebuild. Never overlap anything you might one day connect, because overlapping networks can't be joined at all.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:org block (/12)a /16 per region per environment/20 per tier per AZ100.64/10 secondary block for podsIPAM hands out the rest

Recall

Prompt Answer
Usable addresses in a /24 AWS subnet? 251. Five are reserved in every subnet, whatever its size.
Smallest subnet, and its usable count? /28, 11 usable: the reservation eats 31%.
Three tiers, three AZs: how many subnets? Nine on AWS (zonal subnets), three on GCP (regional).
Pods outgrow a /24. Can you grow it? No. Add a secondary CIDR and new subnets; nothing resizes.
Why avoid 10.0.0.0/16, 172.31.0.0/16, 192.168.0.0/16? Everyone else picked them, so a partner or acquisition will overlap.
Draw by hand: the address plan /12 org → /16 per region-env → /20 per tier per AZ, upper half spare; pods on 100.64.0.0/16.

The idea

A team sizes private subnets at /24, the habit from on-prem racks. The EKS cluster grows to 200 nodes at 30 pods each, and with the AWS VPC CNI every pod holds a VPC address. One AZ needs 2,000 addresses against 251. Pods stick in ContainerCreating in that zone while the other zones look fine, and the only fix is to add space somewhere else.

The trade: a CIDR plan costs an hour before the first VPC exists and saves a migration later. Address space is free, so the only wrong direction is too small.

How it works

The plan as a tree. Each level is carved from the one above and kept apart from everything you might connect to later.

The arithmetic that sets every size:

usable = 2^(32 − prefix) − 5          ← the 5 is constant: network, router, DNS, future, broadcast
subnets = tiers × AZs                  ← 3 × 3 = 9 on AWS; 3 on GCP, where subnets are regional
pod demand ≈ nodes × pods per node     ← 200 × 30 = 6,000; /3 AZs = 2,000 per subnet
prefix delegation: each ENI slot gets a /28  ← 16 addresses per slot instead of 1, so many more pods per node
Rule What actually happens
AZ binding You pick a subnet, the subnet picks the AZ. Free addresses are pooled per subnet, so one AZ can run out while the VPC has thousands spare.
Why split a subnet Only to get a different route table or a different AZ. Separating workloads is a security group's job.
Overlap Two prefixes either intersect or they don't. If they do, no peering, hub or VPN can route between them; only NAT on one side, permanently.
100.64.0.0/10 Shared address space (RFC 6598): not RFC 1918, not on the internet, rarely used by acquired companies. AWS documents it for EKS pod CIDRs.

Evolution

Lineage:1993 CIDR replaces classful addressing (RFC 1519)1996 RFC 1918 private ranges2012 RFC 6598 shared 100.64/102021 VPC CNI prefix delegationDec 2021 Amazon VPC IPAM
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: IPAM turned planning into allocation: teams request a block from a pool instead of choosing one, and non-overlap is enforced.
  • What won't change: CIDRs are immutable once created, so the error cost stays lopsided.

On the wire

Terraform for the plan, with the defaults that bite:

locals {
  vpc_cidr = "10.20.0.0/16"          # from IPAM or the org plan; the console default is 10.0.0.0/16
  pod_cidr = "100.64.0.0/16"         # RFC 6598 space for pods, attached as a secondary block
  azs      = ["ap-south-1a", "ap-south-1b", "ap-south-1c"]
}

resource "aws_subnet" "private" {
  for_each          = toset(local.azs)
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  availability_zone = each.value                        # omit it and AWS picks an AZ for you
  cidr_block        = cidrsubnet(local.vpc_cidr, 4, index(local.azs, each.value) + 1)
  # /16 + 4 bits = /20 → 4,091 usable. Neither this nor the VPC CIDR can ever grow.
}

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): how big is the reservation, and does a per-AZ pod demand fit?

for p in (28, 26, 24, 22, 20, 19):
    n = 2 ** (32 - p); print(f"/{p}: usable {n-5}  tax {5/n:.2%}")
demand = 200 * 30 // 3                 # pods per AZ
# look for: the tax at /28 and whether 2,000 fits a /24
# naive belief predicts: a /24 has 256 addresses and the tax is noise

Run: /28 usable 11, tax 31.25%; /24 251, 1.95%; /20 4,091, 0.12%. 2,000 pods per AZ: a /24 fails, a /20 fits.

Measure it

  • See it: aws ec2 describe-subnets --query 'Subnets[].[CidrBlock,AvailabilityZone,AvailableIpAddressCount]' --output table; python3 -c "import ipaddress as i; print(i.ip_network('10.0.0.0/16').overlaps(i.ip_network('10.0.128.0/17')))".
  • In production: AvailableIpAddressCount per subnet, alert at 20% left; IPAM pool utilisation; any VPC whose CIDR was not allocated by IPAM.
  • Bounded by: pod exhaustion → secondary 100.64 CIDR and prefix delegation; overlap → IPAM-enforced allocation; AZ loss → every tier in at least two AZs.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: AWS subnets are zonal, so three tiers in three AZs is nine subnets, each losing five addresses, and none of them or the VPC CIDR can be resized. I allocate from one organisation-wide plan through IPAM, so nothing I might connect later overlaps. I size private tiers at /20 and put pods on a 100.64 secondary block, because space is free and a rebuild isn't.

Q · Mechanism — Why does capacity fail in one AZ when the VPC has room? Free addresses are pooled per subnet and a subnet is in one AZ. An autoscaler that needs AZ a draws only from AZ a's subnets. So AvailableIpAddressCount can be zero there while the VPC total looks healthy. On GCP the subnet is regional and the pool is shared.

Q · Trade-off — Few large subnets or many small ones? Few large ones: three tiers per AZ, sized generously. Many small subnets pay the five-address tax each, strand addresses in separate pools and multiply route tables and NACLs. Split only when something needs a different route: no NAT, or through an inspection appliance.

Q · Failure — /24 private subnets, and EKS grows. What happens and what do you do? Pods hang in ContainerCreating with "failed to assign an IP address", correlated with one AZ, while the CNI logs show ENI allocation errors. In order: attach a 100.64 secondary CIDR with /19 pod subnets (no rebuild), enable prefix delegation, and size new builds right. You can't grow the /24.

Q · Design — Address plan for three environments in two regions, with acquisitions expected.

  • Org: 10.0.0.0/12 for your own workloads, a /16 per region per environment, with the octet encoding meaning.
  • Inside each /16: /20 per tier per AZ, the upper half left unallocated.
  • Held back: 10.128.0.0/12 reserved for acquisitions and partners; pods on 100.64/10.
  • Enforced: IPAM pools own allocation; alert on any VPC created outside them.

Compare

Subnet Usable (AWS) Typical use Watch out for
/28 11 endpoint or appliance subnets 31% lost to the reservation
/26 59 small public tier for load balancers ALB wants free addresses per AZ to scale
/24 251 instances without pod-per-IP the reflex default; too small for EKS
/20 4,091 private tier default the size that avoids rebuilds
/19+ 8,187+ pod subnets on 100.64 keep pods off the primary CIDR

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Reserved per subnet 5 constant across sizes spec (as of Nov 2026): AWS subnets docs
Subnet sizes allowed /16 to /28 same range as the VPC spec (as of Nov 2026): AWS subnets docs
/24 usable 251 2^8 − 5 derived
/20 usable 4,091 2^12 − 5 derived
Shared address space 100.64.0.0/10 4,194,304 addresses spec: RFC 6598

Pitfalls

  • "Unused address space is waste"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: on-prem, address blocks were scarce and audited.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: inside a VPC nothing is billed for unused private addresses, and too small means a rebuild.
    ↳ Think instead: size for the maximum; being wrong high is free.
  • "You can resize a subnet if you plan carefully"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: most cloud resources are mutable.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: subnets and the primary CIDR are fixed for life; only new blocks can be added.
    ↳ Think instead: every remedy is "allocate elsewhere".
  • Not the same: subnet boundary vs security group
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both look like ways to keep tiers apart.
    ↳ Difference: a subnet gives a different route table and AZ; a security group decides which flows are allowed.
    ↳ Think instead: split subnets for routes, separate workloads with groups.
  • Don't put pods on the primary CIDR.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it works on day one with no extra setup.
    ↳ What goes wrong: pod churn is the most volatile address consumer and drains the tier other workloads share.
    ↳ Do instead: a 100.64 secondary block with dedicated pod subnets.
  • "256 addresses in a /24"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it is the textbook answer, and on-prem you lose only the network and broadcast addresses.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: AWS reserves five per subnet, including the router, the resolver and one held for future use, so 251.
    ↳ Think instead: subtract five every time you quote a size; it is exactly the number a reviewer checks.
  • Shelf life: the arithmetic and immutability are durable; IPAM features and CNI options such as prefix delegation keep moving.

Connections

Path:VPC mental modelsubnets and CIDR planningroute tablespeering
  • Builds on CIDR arithmetic: the prefix notation itself.
  • Owned elsewhere: peering owns what overlap blocks; CNI plugins own how pods draw addresses.
  • Breaks when combined with pod-per-IP networking: demand jumps by pods per node.
  • Bounded by the immutable VPC CIDR: everything here is set once.

notes.title: Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway & Egress — Out Yes, In No, Metered Twice
notes.html:
References

AWS: Internet gateways · AWS: NAT gateways · AWS: Regional NAT gateways · AWS: Attach multiple IPs to a NAT gateway · AWS: Amazon VPC pricing

TL;DR

An internet gateway is the VPC's free, horizontally scaled door to the internet. It translates one private address to one public address, so an instance needs a public IP and a route to it. A NAT gateway lets private subnets reach out without being reachable: it shares its own addresses across thousands of flows by source port. It is metered twice, per hour and per GB processed, on top of internet egress. And it runs out of ports per destination, never of bandwidth first.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:private approute 0.0.0.0/0 → NATNAT rewrites source to its IP and a free portIGWinternetreply hits the NAT's flow tableback to the app

Recall

Prompt Answer
What makes a subnet public? Its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. Nothing else.
Where does a zonal NAT gateway live? In a public subnet: it needs the IGW route itself.
NAT gateway's real ceiling? 55,000 simultaneous connections per destination (IP, port, protocol) per NAT address; up to 8 addresses.
How long does an idle flow hold its port? 350 s, then the NAT drops it silently.
The two NAT meters? Per hour and per GB processed, plus internet egress on the same bytes.
Draw by hand: the egress path app (private) → NAT in public subnet of the same AZ → IGW → vendor; S3 bypasses it through a gateway endpoint.

The idea

A fleet of 1,200 pods each holds 45 connections to one vendor API at 203.0.113.10:443. That's 54,000 flows to a single destination through one NAT address. Bandwidth is at 2%, and yet connections start timing out at peak, so the vendor gets blamed. The metric that would have explained it, ErrorPortAllocation, isn't on any default dashboard.

A NAT gateway tells flows apart only by source port, and a port can be reused only for a different destination. So the limit is set by how concentrated your traffic is, not by how much of it there is.

The trade: NAT gives private workloads the whole internet with no inbound exposure, and you pay with two meters, a port ceiling per destination and no idea which hostname anything called.

How it works

One outbound connection (app 10.20.16.42, NAT address 52.0.2.10, vendor 203.0.113.10:443). The way back exists only because NAT remembered the flow.

Box Translation Scope and cost
Internet gateway 1:1, an instance's private IP ↔ its own public IP one per VPC, free, no bandwidth limit you will meet
NAT gateway, zonal many:1 by source port one AZ; hourly + per GB; 5 Gbps scaling to 100 Gbps
NAT gateway, regional (Nov 2025) same one gateway that expands into AZs as workloads appear, up to 60 min to reach a new AZ; no private NAT
Egress-only IGW none (IPv6 is public) outbound-initiated only, free

The ceiling, in numbers:

flows to ONE destination ≤ 55,000 × NAT addresses       ← 1 IP: 55,000 · 8 IPs: 440,000
ports held by abandoned flows = new flows/s × 350 s       ← 158/s never closed → 55,300 > 55,000
cost per GB out = NAT processing + internet egress        ← + cross-AZ if the NAT is in another zone

Evolution

Lineage:NAT instances you ran yourselfDec 2015 managed NAT gatewayFeb 2023 up to 8 IPs per NAT gatewayFeb 2024 every public IPv4 address billed hourlyNov 2025 regional NAT gateway
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: the regional mode removes "one gateway and one route table per AZ" for most designs; zonal stays for private NAT and tight per-AZ control.
  • What won't change: port translation, so a per-destination ceiling and a stateful flow table.

On the wire

Terraform for zonal NAT per AZ, the shape most existing estates still run:

resource "aws_internet_gateway" "igw" { vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id }   # free, nothing to size

resource "aws_nat_gateway" "nat" {
  for_each                       = aws_subnet.public              # one per AZ
  allocation_id                  = aws_eip.nat[each.key].id
  secondary_allocation_ids       = [aws_eip.nat2[each.key].id]    # +55,000 per destination
  subnet_id                      = each.value.id                  # MUST be a public subnet
}                                # default quota: 2 EIPs per public NAT gateway; more needs a request

resource "aws_route_table" "private" {
  for_each = aws_subnet.private
  vpc_id   = aws_vpc.main.id
  route {
    cidr_block     = "0.0.0.0/0"
    nat_gateway_id = aws_nat_gateway.nat[each.key].id  # same AZ, or every byte also pays cross-AZ
  }
}

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): when do abandoned connections exhaust one destination?

for rate in (100, 158, 200):              # new connections per second, never closed
    held = rate * 350                       # each holds its port for the idle timeout
    print(rate, held, held > 55_000)
# look for: the rate where held ports cross 55,000
# naive belief predicts: NAT scales to 100 Gbps, so a few hundred connections a second can't matter

Run: 100/s holds 35,000 (fine); 158/s holds 55,300 (over); 200/s holds 70,000. Keepalive pooling removes it; bandwidth never enters.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -s https://checkip.amazonaws.com from a private instance prints the NAT's public IP; ss -tn state established '( dport = :443 )' | wc -l counts flows to one port.
  • In production: NAT ErrorPortAllocation (must stay 0), IdleTimeoutCount, BytesOutToDestination vs a flat request count; cross-AZ bytes to the NAT.
  • Bounded by: port exhaustion → connection reuse, more NAT addresses, more destinations; NAT cost → VPC endpoints; "what did we call" → a forward proxy (posture).

Tech discussion

30-second answer: An internet gateway does 1:1 translation for instances that have public IPs, and a subnet is public only because its default route points at one. A NAT gateway lets private subnets connect out by sharing its address across flows by source port. It's stateful, so replies come back and nothing unsolicited gets in. It's metered hourly and per GB on top of egress, and its limit is 55,000 flows per destination per address.

Q · Mechanism — Why does an instance with a public IP in a private subnet have no internet? An address is not a path. The IGW translates only traffic routed to it, and this subnet's default route points at NAT. Conversely, an instance in an IGW-routed subnet with no public IP has nothing to translate to. Internet access needs both.

Q · Trade-off — One NAT gateway for three AZs, one per AZ, or regional? A single zonal gateway makes one AZ a dependency for all egress, and two thirds of bytes pay cross-AZ on top of NAT processing. Per-AZ zonal fixes both at an extra hourly charge and needs a route table per AZ. Since Nov 2025, a regional NAT gateway gives the same in-zone, multi-AZ result with one gateway and one route. I'd pick it for new builds unless I need private NAT.

Q · Failure — Intermittent timeouts to one vendor at peak; bandwidth is low. What is it? Port exhaustion: ErrorPortAllocation above zero and IdleTimeoutCount rising, correlated with concurrency, not bytes. Fix in order: pool and reuse connections with keepalive under 350 s, add secondary NAT addresses, split subnets across gateways. A bigger anything doesn't help.

Q · Design — Egress for AI agents that call arbitrary third-party APIs, with per-tenant audit.

  • No direct route: agent subnets have no NAT route at all.
  • Proxy hop: egress goes to an internal LB in front of a forward-proxy tier that holds the per-tenant hostname allow-lists and the audit log.
  • NAT behind the proxy: only proxy subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to NAT.
  • Endpoints for AWS: S3, ECR and Secrets Manager go through endpoints, so the proxy log shows only external calls.
  • Watch: ErrorPortAllocation, NAT bytes vs request count, denials per tenant.

Compare

Internet gateway NAT gateway Egress-only IGW Forward proxy
Direction both outbound-initiated outbound-initiated (IPv6) outbound-initiated
Needs public IP on instance yes no no no
Cost free hourly + per GB free your compute
Sees hostnames no no no yes
Ceiling none you'll meet 55,000 per destination per IP none you'll meet your ephemeral ports
Pick it for inbound-reachable tiers private workloads going out IPv6 workloads controlled, audited egress

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Flows per destination per NAT IP 55,000 destination = IP, port, protocol default (as of Nov 2026): AWS NAT gateway docs
IPs per NAT gateway up to 8 (1 + 7) 440,000 per destination default (as of Nov 2026): AWS NAT gateway docs
NAT idle timeout 350 s dropped silently, no RST to the app default (as of Nov 2026): AWS NAT gateway docs
NAT bandwidth 5 Gbps, scales to 100 Gbps rarely the limit default (as of Nov 2026): AWS NAT gateway docs
Regional NAT expansion to a new AZ up to 60 min after a workload appears there default (as of Nov 2026): AWS regional NAT docs
Abandoned flows to hit the ceiling 158 per second 158 × 350 = 55,300 derived

Pitfalls

  • "The internet gateway is a bottleneck to size"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every on-prem edge router had a capacity number.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it is horizontally scaled, redundant and free, with one per VPC and nothing to configure.
    ↳ Think instead: every egress limit and cost lives on the NAT gateway, so look there first.
  • "A NAT gateway is a firewall"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: nothing unsolicited gets in through it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: that's a side effect of the flow table. It allows every outbound destination and logs only addresses.
    ↳ Think instead: NAT is connectivity; policy is security groups and a hostname-aware proxy.
  • "One NAT gateway is the cheap option"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it saves two hourly charges on the bill line you can see.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: most egress then crosses AZs and pays per GB in both directions, and one zone takes all egress down.
    ↳ Think instead: price the per-GB meters, then pick per-AZ or regional.
  • Not the same: NAT gateway vs forward proxy
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both sit on the way out and hide private addresses.
    ↳ Difference: NAT rewrites addresses at L3/L4; a proxy terminates the request and sees the hostname.
    ↳ Think instead: NAT for reach, proxy for control, chained proxy → NAT.
  • Don't send S3 or DynamoDB traffic through NAT.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it already works, because those services resolve to public IPs.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every byte pays NAT processing for traffic that never leaves AWS.
    ↳ Do instead: a free gateway endpoint, one route-table entry.
  • Shelf life: port translation and the per-destination ceiling are durable; regional NAT, IP counts, bandwidth and prices keep moving.

Connections

Path:route tablesIGW, NAT and egressendpointsthe bill
  • Builds on NAT: port address translation before its cloud form.
  • Owned elsewhere: route tables own the public/private definition; the bill owns the meters.
  • Breaks when combined with idle timeouts: a pooled connection quiet for 350 s is dead.
  • Bounded by egress security for agents: the proxy layer above NAT.

notes.title: Route Tables — Longest Prefix Wins, and the Main Table Catches the Rest
notes.html:
References

AWS: Route table concepts · AWS: Configure route tables · AWS: Example routing options

TL;DR

A route table is a list of destination prefixes and targets attached to subnets. For each packet the most specific matching prefix wins, whatever order the rows are in. Every table has an undeletable local route for the VPC CIDR, so anything inside the VPC is always reachable. Everything else (internet, NAT, peering, endpoints, hub) is a row someone added. A subnet with no explicit association silently uses the VPC's main table.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper packet
Flow:packet leaves ENIsubnet's table (or the main table)all matching prefixeslongest winstarget: local, IGW, NAT, pcx, tgw, vpceno match: dropped

Recall

Prompt Answer
10.30.0.0/16 → pcx and 10.30.5.7/32 → tgw: where does 10.30.5.7 go? The TGW: a /32 beats a /16, row order is irrelevant.
Can you delete or override the local route? Not delete. You can point a more specific subnet route at an appliance for inspection, but the VPC CIDR always stays reachable.
A subnet's association is removed. What does it route with? The main route table, which may well have an IGW route.

The idea

To "cut off" a compromised subnet, someone deletes its route-table association. The subnet now uses the main route table, and the main table was the one the original VPC wizard gave an internet-gateway route. The isolation step just made the subnet public.

There is no "no table" state: a subnet always has some table. The trade: routing by table gives you one place to decide every subnet's reach, and you pay with a silent fallback that does the opposite of what removing a thing usually means.

How it works

Four destinations, one table (10.20.0.0/16 local, 10.30.0.0/16 pcx, 10.30.5.7/32 tgw, 0.0.0.0/0 nat); the most specific prefix wins.

Rule What actually happens
Longest prefix Among matching rows, the longest prefix wins; ties between a static route and a propagated one go to the static route.
local Present in every table for every VPC CIDR. It can't be deleted, which is why a VPC is one L3 domain.
Main table Every VPC has one, and it is used by any subnet without an explicit association. Keep it with no default route.
Tier labels 0.0.0.0/0 → igw is public, → nat is private, no default route is isolated. Owned by egress.
Gateway route tables A table can also attach to an IGW or VGW (edge association) to steer inbound traffic through an appliance first.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: "more specific routes" inside the VPC CIDR let a subnet-to-subnet path go through a firewall appliance; managed prefix lists let one row name many CIDRs.
  • What won't change: longest-prefix match, the same rule every IP router uses (routing basics).

On the wire

Terraform, with the default that bites:

resource "aws_default_route_table" "main" {        # take control of the MAIN table
  default_route_table_id = aws_vpc.main.default_route_table_id
  # no routes: an unassociated subnet now reaches only the VPC, not the internet
}

resource "aws_route_table_association" "app_a" {   # every subnet gets an explicit one
  subnet_id      = aws_subnet.private["ap-south-1a"].id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.private["ap-south-1a"].id
}

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026), longest-prefix match with ipaddress:

rt = {"10.20.0.0/16": "local", "0.0.0.0/0": "nat-a",
      "10.30.0.0/16": "pcx-staging", "10.30.5.7/32": "tgw"}
best = max((n for n in map(ip_network, rt) if ip_address(dst) in n), key=lambda n: n.prefixlen)
# look for: which target 10.30.5.7 and 10.30.5.8 get
# naive belief predicts: first matching row wins, so both go to pcx-staging

Run: 10.30.5.7 → tgw, 10.30.5.8 → pcx-staging, 10.20.17.88 → local, 8.8.8.8 → nat-a.

Measure it

  • See it: aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=association.subnet-id,Values=<subnet> returns nothing for a subnet on the main table; VPC Reachability Analyzer shows the hop that matched.
  • In production: a config rule that alerts on any subnet without an explicit association, and on a main table with 0.0.0.0/0.
  • Bounded by: route quotas per table (raisable) → summarise prefixes or use prefix lists; fallback surprises → an empty main table.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A route table maps destination prefixes to targets, and the longest matching prefix wins regardless of order. Every table has a local route for the VPC CIDR, which is why everything inside a VPC can reach everything else. Public, private and isolated are just the target of 0.0.0.0/0. An unassociated subnet falls back to the main table, so I keep that table empty and associate every subnet explicitly.

Q · Mechanism — Why can't you express "try the peering, then fall back to the hub"? There's no ordering, only specificity, and no health-based failover between rows. One prefix has one target in a table. Failover needs a dynamic source: BGP propagation from a VPN or Direct Connect, or a hub that knows path state.

Q · Trade-off — One route table per AZ or one shared private table? Per AZ when each AZ's default route targets its own zonal NAT gateway. One shared table is fine with a regional NAT gateway, endpoints only, or no egress at all. Fewer tables are easier to audit, so the target decides the count.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Tables a subnet uses exactly 1 explicit, or the main table spec (as of Nov 2026): AWS route table docs
Model: /32 vs /16 for 10.30.5.7 /32 wins order of rows irrelevant derived

Pitfalls

  • "Routes are evaluated top to bottom like firewall rules"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: NACLs, iptables and most ACLs are ordered lists.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: routing picks the most specific match; a /32 added anywhere overrides a /16 silently.
    ↳ Think instead: sort by prefix length in your head, never by row position.
  • Don't remove an association to isolate a subnet.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: removing the link feels like cutting the cable.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the subnet falls back to the main table, which may route to an internet gateway.
    ↳ Do instead: associate an explicit table with no default route.
  • Not the same: route table vs security group
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both decide "can A reach B".
    ↳ Difference: a route decides whether a path exists; a security group decides whether a flow on that path is allowed.
    ↳ Think instead: no route beats deny: a missing path can't be loosened by a rule change.
  • "The local route can be removed to split a VPC"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every other row in the table can be edited or deleted.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: local is fixed for each VPC CIDR, so two subnets in one VPC can always route to each other.
    ↳ Think instead: split with security groups and NACLs, or put the workloads in separate VPCs.
  • Shelf life: longest-prefix match is permanent; target types and quotas change.

Connections

Path:subnetsroute tablesIGW, NAT and egressTransit Gateway
  • Builds on routing basics: longest-prefix match.
  • Owned elsewhere: egress owns what each default-route target does.
  • Breaks when combined with overlapping CIDRs: one prefix can't have two targets.
  • Bounded by SG vs NACL: a route makes traffic possible, a rule makes it allowed.

notes.title: Security Groups vs NACLs — Stateful on the ENI, Stateless on the Subnet
notes.html:
References

AWS: Security groups · AWS: Network ACLs · AWS: Security group connection tracking · AWS: Security group referencing for Transit Gateway · Microsoft Learn: Network security groups

TL;DR

A security group is a stateful allow-list on a network interface. Allow the connection in, and its replies go back out because the flow is tracked. A network ACL is a stateless, numbered rule list on a subnet. It can deny, and it judges every packet in each direction separately. Allow inbound 443 but forget the outbound ephemeral range, and the request arrives while the reply is dropped. Security groups do the real work, because a group can name another group as its source. NACLs are kept for coarse subnet-wide denies.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:packet enters subnetNACL inbound, lowest rule number firstSG on the ENIflow trackedreply leaves ENI (no SG check)NACL outbound, judged againclient

Recall

Prompt Answer
The one-line difference? SG: stateful, ENI, allow-only. NACL: stateless, subnet, allow and deny, first match by rule number.
Why does a NACL need 1024–65535 outbound? The reply goes to the client's ephemeral port, and the NACL doesn't remember the request.
What can an SG source be that a NACL's can't? Another security group: identity, not IP range.
New SG vs default NACL? New SG: no inbound, all outbound. Default NACL: allow all both ways. A new custom NACL: deny all.
You delete the SG rule behind an open connection. Does it drop? Not at once: a tracked flow keeps going until it idles out. Untracked flows stop immediately.
Draw by hand: one HTTPS request NACL in (443) → SG (443 from LB-SG, tracked) → app → SG out (free) → NACL out (1024–65535) → client.

The idea

Someone locks down a subnet's NACL to "only 443 in, only 443 out", which looks symmetric and tidy. Health checks start failing. The SYN reaches the instance and the instance answers, but the reply is a packet to the load balancer's port 51544, and no outbound rule allows 51544. A security group would have let it through, because it remembers that the reply belongs to an allowed connection. A NACL remembers nothing.

The trade: a NACL buys explicit deny at the subnet edge, and you pay by writing every return path by hand, which usually opens a far wider port range than the rule you meant.

How it works

One HTTPS request, the checks it passes, and the one that kills the reply.

Rule Security group Network ACL
Attached to an ENI (instance, LB, endpoint, Lambda in a VPC) a subnet; traffic within the subnet never hits it
State tracked: replies allowed automatically none: each direction judged alone
Rule logic allow-only; all rules of all attached groups are unioned allow and deny; lowest rule number that matches wins, then * deny
Source can be CIDR, prefix list, another SG (same VPC, a peered VPC in-region, or across a Transit Gateway since Sep 2024) CIDR only
Change to a rule new flows obey at once; existing tracked flows continue until idle every packet obeys at once

Tracking is what makes "stateful" true, and it has edges:

flow untracked ⇐ inbound AND outbound allow all traffic from/to 0.0.0.0/0      ← no state kept, rule removal cuts it now
tracked TCP established idle timeout = 432,000 s (5 days)                      ← 350 s on Nitro v6; configurable per ENI
NACL return range ≥ the client's ephemeral range                               ← Linux 32768–60999, Windows 49152–65535, so 1024–65535

Evolution

Lineage:Aug 2009 VPC launches with security groups and network ACLsNov 2023 configurable connection-tracking timeoutsSep 2024 SG referencing across Transit Gateway (inbound rules only)
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: SG-references-SG now works across a Transit Gateway, so moving off peering no longer means falling back to CIDR rules.
  • What won't change: state lives on the ENI, so the subnet-level control stays stateless.

On the wire

Terraform for the app tier, with the defaults that bite:

resource "aws_security_group" "app" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
  # Terraform REMOVES the default allow-all egress rule on SGs it manages;
  # the console and API keep it. Declare egress explicitly either way.
}

resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "from_lb" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.app.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.lb.id   # identity, not a CIDR
  from_port                    = 443
  to_port                      = 443
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
}

resource "aws_network_acl_rule" "out_ephemeral" {   # the rule people forget
  network_acl_id = aws_network_acl.app.id
  rule_number    = 120          # lowest matching number wins; leave gaps of 10
  egress         = true
  protocol       = "tcp"
  rule_action    = "allow"
  cidr_block     = "10.20.0.0/16"
  from_port      = 1024
  to_port        = 65535
}

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): the same request through a mirrored NACL and through a tracked SG.

nacl_out = [(100, "allow", 443), (200, "deny", None)]   # "443 out" mirrors "443 in"
syn = ("198.51.100.7", 51544, "10.20.0.10", 443)
print(nacl(nacl_out, syn[1]))                            # the reply goes TO port 51544
print("allow" if syn in tracked else "deny")             # SG: is this a known flow?
# look for: NACL outbound verdict on the reply
# naive belief predicts: allow, because 443 is allowed both ways

Run: NACL inbound SYN allow, NACL outbound reply deny, SG reply allow.

Measure it

  • See it: VPC flow logs with action and log-status: an ACCEPT inbound record followed by a REJECT outbound on the same 5-tuple is a NACL return-path miss; aws ec2 describe-network-acls shows the numbered rules.
  • In production: flow-log REJECT counts per ENI; conntrack_allowance_exceeded in the ENA driver stats (ethtool -S eth0) when tracked flows outgrow the instance's table.
  • Bounded by: wide NACL ranges → keep NACLs coarse and let SGs carry policy; conntrack exhaustion → untracked rules or a larger instance; stale access → rotate and delete rules knowing tracked flows linger.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A security group is stateful and sits on the ENI: allow the inbound connection and replies flow back because it's tracked. It's allow-only, and it can name another security group as the source, which is the real reason it carries policy. A NACL is stateless and sits on the subnet. It evaluates numbered allow and deny rules per direction, so every return path needs the ephemeral range. I use NACLs only for coarse denies.

Q · Mechanism — What does "stateful" mean in implementation terms? The hypervisor keeps a connection-tracking table per ENI. A packet that matches a tracked flow skips rule evaluation in the other direction. That table is finite, has idle timeouts (5 days for established TCP by default), and isn't used at all when rules allow all traffic both ways.

Q · Trade-off — When would you reach for a NACL at all? When I need a deny: block one hostile CIDR during an incident, or guarantee a data subnet can never talk to a range even if someone adds an SG rule. That second use is the real one: a guard rail owned by a different team than the one editing SGs. For everyday app-to-app policy, SG referencing beats any CIDR rule.

Q · Failure — Requests time out but the instance logs show them arriving. Cause? A missing NACL outbound ephemeral rule, or an asymmetric return path. The SYN is accepted and the reply is dropped at the subnet edge. Flow logs show an inbound ACCEPT and an outbound REJECT for the same flow. The fix is an outbound 1024–65535 rule scoped to the client's CIDR, not 0.0.0.0/0.

Q · Design — Firewalling for a three-tier app with a compliance boundary on the data tier.

  • Policy: SGs by role. LB-SG allows 443 from the internet, App-SG allows 443 from LB-SG, DB-SG allows 5432 from App-SG. No CIDRs inside the VPC.
  • Guard rail: the data subnets' NACL denies everything except the app subnets' CIDRs and their return range, owned by security, not the app team.
  • Exposure: the isolated subnets have no default route at all (route tables), and VPC Block Public Access is on.
  • Evidence: flow logs to a central account, with alerts on REJECT spikes per ENI.

Compare

AWS SG AWS NACL GCP firewall rules Azure NSG
State stateful stateless stateful stateful
Scope ENI subnet network, targeted by tag or service account NIC or subnet
Deny no yes yes, by priority yes, by priority
Identity source another SG no service account or tag application security group

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Tracked TCP established idle timeout 432,000 s (5 days) 350 s on Nitro v6; 60–432,000 configurable default (as of Nov 2026): AWS connection tracking docs
Linux client ephemeral range 32768–60999 net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range default (as of Nov 2026): Linux kernel
NACL return range to allow 1024–65535 covers Linux, Windows and ELB clients default (as of Nov 2026): AWS Network ACLs docs
NACL evaluation lowest number first, first match wins then the * deny spec (as of Nov 2026): AWS Network ACLs docs

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: security group vs NACL
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "firewall rules" on the same VPC console page.
    ↳ Difference: an SG is stateful, allow-only, on the ENI, and can name other SGs; a NACL is stateless, ordered, on the subnet, and can deny.
    ↳ Think instead: SGs for policy, NACLs for a few coarse denies.
  • "NACLs are the stricter layer, so the stronger control"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: explicit deny and subnet scope sound more locked down.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: statelessness forces 1024–65535 open in the return direction, so a "tight" NACL admits a wide range.
    ↳ Think instead: the SG is usually the narrower filter; judge by what is actually open.
  • "Deleting an SG rule cuts the connections it allowed"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: changes to the rule list apply to new packets immediately.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: tracked flows keep going until they idle out, up to 5 days for established TCP by default; only untracked flows stop at once.
    ↳ Think instead: in an incident, add a NACL deny or stop the process, because that cuts every packet.
  • Don't mirror inbound ports on NACL outbound rules.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "443 in, 443 out" looks symmetric and minimal.
    ↳ What goes wrong: replies go to the client's ephemeral port, so every response is dropped and it looks like a dead app.
    ↳ Do instead: allow 1024–65535 outbound to the client CIDR.
  • "Security groups can carve an exception with a deny"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: most firewalls have deny rules and ordering.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: SGs are allow-only and every attached group's rules are unioned, so there is no "allow the range except this host".
    ↳ Think instead: express exceptions as a NACL deny, or shrink the allow.
  • Shelf life: stateful vs stateless is durable; conntrack timeouts, cross-TGW referencing and quotas move.

Connections

Path:IGW, NAT and egressSG vs NACLpeeringposture
  • Builds on sockets and the ephemeral range: why replies target high ports.
  • Owned elsewhere: route tables own reachability; network policies own pod-level filtering.
  • Breaks when combined with pod-per-IP CNIs: many pods share one node's SG unless per-pod SGs are on.
  • Bounded by posture: SGs and NACLs are two of several layers.

notes.title: VPC Peering — One Pair, Non-Transitive, No Overlap
notes.html:
References

AWS: How VPC peering connections work · AWS: VPC peering connection quotas · AWS whitepaper: VPC peering at scale

TL;DR

Peering is a direct private L3 link between exactly two VPCs, in one region or across regions. There's no appliance in the path and no bandwidth ceiling of its own. Two rules define it. It's non-transitive: A↔B and B↔C never gives A↔C, and A can't use B's NAT, internet gateway or VPN either. And it refuses overlapping CIDRs outright. So n VPCs need n(n−1)/2 peerings plus routes on both sides of each, which is why peering suits a handful of VPCs and a hub suits more.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:requestacceptroute peer CIDR → pcx in BOTH VPCsSG rule on the receiving sidetraffic flowsnothing beyond the peer's own CIDR

Recall

Prompt Answer
A↔B and B↔C are peered. Can A reach C? No. Each pair needs its own peering and routes.
Ten VPCs in a full mesh: how many peerings and route edits? 45 peerings, 90 route entries.
What else blocks a peering besides overlap? Nothing technical; but accepting it moves no traffic until both route tables and SGs allow it.

The idea

A platform team peers every workload VPC to a shared-services VPC that holds the NAT gateways and the VPN to the office. The workloads can reach shared services, but they can't reach the internet through its NAT or the office through its VPN. Peering carries traffic for the peer's CIDR only, never onward through the peer's gateways.

The trade: peering is the cheapest, fastest link between two VPCs, and you pay with a mesh that grows quadratically and no way to share one VPC's gateways with another.

How it works

Three VPCs, two peerings, one missing path.

Rule What actually happens
Non-transitive a packet arriving over a peering is delivered only to the peer VPC's own CIDR; no edge-to-edge routing through its IGW, NAT, VPN or gateway endpoints
Overlap any intersecting CIDR, primary or secondary, blocks creation (CIDR planning)
Routes both sides add peer CIDR → pcx-…; a more specific route can expose only some subnets
SG referencing a rule can name the peer's SG within one region; across regions, CIDRs only
Cost no hourly or per-GB charge for the link; same-AZ traffic over it is free, cross-AZ and cross-region transfer still bill 
peerings for a full mesh = n(n − 1) / 2     ← 10 VPCs: 45 · 50: 1,225 · 100: 4,950
route entries           = n(n − 1)          ← one per side
hub attachments         = n                 ← the reason a hub exists

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): Mar 2014 launch, inter-region peering since Nov 2017.
  • Changed recently: cross-Transit-Gateway SG referencing (Sep 2024) removed peering's last unique advantage for many designs; it remains the zero-cost path for heavy pairs.
  • What won't change: non-transitivity, which is a property of how the fabric delivers, not a setting.

On the wire

Terraform for one peering, with the default that bites:

resource "aws_vpc_peering_connection" "a_b" {
  vpc_id      = aws_vpc.a.id
  peer_vpc_id = aws_vpc.b.id
  auto_accept = true          # same account and region only; otherwise an accepter resource is needed
}
# Accepting moves NOTHING until both sides have a route:
resource "aws_route" "a_to_b" {
  route_table_id            = aws_route_table.a_private.id
  destination_cidr_block    = "10.1.0.0/16"
  vpc_peering_connection_id = aws_vpc_peering_connection.a_b.id
}                             # …and the mirror route in VPC B, and an SG rule on the receiver

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): overlap and mesh growth.

print(ip_network("10.0.0.0/16").overlaps(ip_network("10.0.128.0/17")))
for n in (5, 10, 50, 100): print(n, n*(n-1)//2, n*(n-1), n)
# look for: overlap True, and the mesh column against the hub column
# naive belief predicts: "/17 is half the size, so it fits beside"; mesh growth is linear

Run: True; 10 VPCs need 45 peerings and 90 routes, 100 need 4,950 and 9,900, against 100 hub attachments.

Measure it

  • See it: aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections shows status active; Reachability Analyzer from an ENI in A to one in C names the missing hop.
  • In production: peerings per VPC against the quota; flow-log REJECT on the receiving ENI after a new peering (SG not updated).
  • Bounded by: the quota of 50 per VPC (raisable to 125) and the mesh's route edits → Transit Gateway.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Peering is a private L3 link between two VPCs over the provider's backbone, with no appliance and no link charge. It's non-transitive and refuses overlapping CIDRs, so a mesh grows as n(n−1)/2 and you can't share one VPC's NAT or VPN through it. I use it for a few VPCs or one heavy pair, and a Transit Gateway beyond that.

Q · Mechanism — Why is peering non-transitive? The fabric delivers peered traffic only to destinations inside the peer VPC's CIDRs. It doesn't re-route it through the peer's route table to another attachment. So there's no path to C or to B's gateways, whatever routes you add in B.

Q · Trade-off — Peering or Transit Gateway for twenty VPCs? A hub: 20 attachments instead of 190 peerings, central segmentation, shared egress and VPN. Keep a direct peering beside it for the two or three highest-volume pairs, because peering has no per-GB processing charge.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Active peerings per VPC 50, raisable to 125 pending requests: 25 default (as of Nov 2026): AWS peering quotas
Mesh of 10 / 100 VPCs 45 / 4,950 peerings n(n−1)/2 derived
Link charge none transfer charges still apply default (as of Nov 2026): AWS VPC pricing

Pitfalls

  • "Peering A to B gives A everything B can reach"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: in a normal router network, a link plus routes is transitive.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: A reaches B's CIDR only: not B's peers, NAT, internet gateway, VPN or gateway endpoints.
    ↳ Think instead: one peering, one CIDR; shared gateways need a hub.
  • "Peering has a throughput bottleneck"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: VPNs and appliances do, and the console shows a connection object.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: there's no device in the path; flows run at instance network speed.
    ↳ Think instead: move to a hub for topology and policy, never for bandwidth.
  • Not the same: peering vs PrivateLink
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both connect two VPCs privately.
    ↳ Difference: peering joins whole CIDRs both ways and needs no overlap; PrivateLink exposes one service one way and works with overlapping CIDRs.
    ↳ Think instead: network join or service exposure? (endpoints).
  • Don't stop at "accepted".
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the console shows the peering as active and green.
    ↳ What goes wrong: without routes on both sides and an SG rule on the receiver, nothing flows and it looks broken.
    ↳ Do instead: add the route pair and the SG rule in the same change.
  • Shelf life: non-transitivity and overlap refusal are durable; quotas and pricing details move.

Connections

Path:CIDR planningVPC peeringTransit GatewayPrivateLink
  • Builds on route tables: a peering is a route target.
  • Owned elsewhere: CIDR planning owns overlap avoidance.
  • Breaks when combined with overlapping secondary CIDRs: one shared 100.64 block on both sides blocks the peering.
  • Bounded by the bill: free link, but cross-AZ and cross-region bytes still bill.

notes.title: Transit Gateway — A Regional Hub, Segmented by Route Table
notes.html:
References

AWS: What is a transit gateway? · AWS: Transit Gateway quotas · AWS: NAT gateways with multiple VPCs at scale · AWS: Transit Gateway pricing

TL;DR

A Transit Gateway is a regional router you attach VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect gateways to, once each. Connectivity becomes n attachments instead of a n(n−1)/2 mesh, and it's transitive by design. Who reaches whom is decided by the hub's own route tables. An attachment associates with one table, which decides where its packets can go. It propagates into others, which decides who can reach it. Every attachment bills by the hour and every byte through the hub bills per GB, so heavy pairs often keep a direct peering beside it.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper packet
Flow:VPC route 10.0.0.0/8 → tgwattachment ENI in each AZthe attachment's associated TGW tablelongest prefixtarget attachmentdestination VPC

Recall

Prompt Answer
Association vs propagation? Association: which TGW table my traffic is looked up in. Propagation: which tables learn a route to me.
Prod must never reach dev; both reach shared services. How? Prod and dev associate with separate tables; shared services propagates into both; neither propagates into the other's.
Does a hub fix overlapping CIDRs? No. A prefix still has one target per table.

The idea

A company has 30 VPCs and a growing peering mesh nobody can draw. A Transit Gateway replaces it with 30 attachments. Then the first audit asks "can dev reach prod?" and the answer is yes: every attachment was associated with the default route table, and every attachment propagated into it.

The hub made connectivity easy, and the default makes it total. Segmentation is extra work you have to add on purpose.

The trade: a hub turns a mesh into a star with central policy, and you pay with an hourly fee per attachment, a per-GB fee on every crossing, and a default route table that connects everything to everything.

How it works

Two route tables turn one hub into two segments that share a services VPC.

Rule What actually happens
Default table new attachments associate with and propagate into it unless you turn both defaults off: full mesh by default
Segmentation prod propagates only into rt-prod and rt-shared; dev only into rt-dev and rt-shared; so prod and dev have no route to each other
Appliance mode for a stateful firewall VPC, keeps both directions of a flow in the same AZ; off by default, and asymmetric paths drop flows
SG referencing across the hub since Sep 2024, inbound rules only, enabled on the TGW and on each attachment
Between regions TGW peering, static routes only

Evolution

Lineage:Nov 2018 Transit GatewayDec 2019 inter-region TGW peeringJul 2022 Cloud WAN (policy-defined global network on top)Sep 2024 SG referencing across the hub
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: Cloud WAN for multi-region estates; per-AZ attachment bandwidth now up to 100 Gbps.
  • What won't change: a hub is a router, so overlap stays fatal and every hop through it is a meter.

On the wire

Terraform for a segmented hub, with the defaults that bite:

resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway" "hub" {
  default_route_table_association = "disable"   # default "enable": every attachment joins one table
  default_route_table_propagation = "disable"   # default "enable": …and everyone learns everyone
  security_group_referencing_support = "enable" # default "disable" on the TGW
}

resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table_association" "prod" {
  transit_gateway_attachment_id  = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment.prod.id
  transit_gateway_route_table_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table.prod.id
}

resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table_propagation" "shared_into_prod" {
  transit_gateway_attachment_id  = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment.shared.id
  transit_gateway_route_table_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table.prod.id
}

Measure it

  • See it: aws ec2 search-transit-gateway-routes --transit-gateway-route-table-id <rt-prod> --filters Name=type,Values=propagated lists who prod can reach; a dev CIDR there is a segmentation bug.
  • In production: BytesIn/BytesOut and PacketDropCountNoRoute per attachment; attachment count against quota; TGW processed GB as a bill line.
  • Bounded by: per-GB cost on heavy pairs → a direct peering beside the hub; asymmetric firewall paths → appliance mode.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A Transit Gateway is a regional hub: each VPC attaches once and the hub's route tables decide reachability, so it's transitive and scales linearly. Segmentation comes from separate tables: an attachment associates with one table and propagates into the ones that should reach it. It bills per attachment-hour and per GB, so I keep direct peerings for the heaviest pairs.

Q · Mechanism — How does a packet find its way through the hub? The source VPC's route table sends the prefix to the TGW attachment ENI in that AZ. The hub looks the destination up in the table the source attachment is associated with, and the longest prefix names the target attachment. The packet then enters the target VPC through that attachment's ENI, preferring the same AZ.

Q · Trade-off — Centralise egress through a hub or NAT per VPC? Central egress puts one NAT tier and one inspection point in front of many VPCs: fewer gateways, one allow-list, one log. You pay TGW processing on every egress byte plus an extra hop. Above roughly ten VPCs, or with a filtering requirement, central wins. For one or two heavy VPCs, local NAT is cheaper.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Attachments per TGW 5,000 one VPC attachment per VPC per TGW default (as of Nov 2026): AWS TGW quotas
Bandwidth per VPC attachment per AZ up to 100 Gbps more via AWS account team default (as of Nov 2026): AWS TGW quotas
Charges per attachment-hour + per GB processed both directions through the hub default (as of Nov 2026): AWS TGW pricing

Pitfalls

  • "Attaching a VPC connects it to the others"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: with the defaults on, it does.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: reachability comes from association and propagation, which are separate; with defaults off, a new attachment reaches nothing.
    ↳ Think instead: name both tables for every attachment in review.
  • Don't keep the default route table in a segmented design.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's already there and everything works.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every new attachment joins a full mesh, so dev reaches prod the day it attaches.
    ↳ Do instead: disable default association and propagation and attach to named tables.
  • "A Transit Gateway replaces peering"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it does everything peering does and more.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: peering has no per-GB processing charge, so a heavy pair through the hub can cost more than everything else.
    ↳ Think instead: hub for breadth, peering for volume, side by side.
  • Not the same: TGW route table vs VPC route table
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "route tables" with prefixes and targets.
    ↳ Difference: a VPC table sends traffic to the hub; the hub's table decides which attachment it goes to next.
    ↳ Think instead: two lookups, two owners: the VPC team and the network team.
  • Shelf life: association, propagation and the star topology are durable; quotas, bandwidth and Cloud WAN features move.

Connections

Path:peeringTransit Gatewaymulti-regionVPN and Direct Connect
  • Builds on route tables: the same longest-prefix rule, twice.
  • Owned elsewhere: egress owns NAT behaviour in the central egress VPC.
  • Breaks when combined with stateful firewalls without appliance mode: the return path lands in another AZ.
  • Bounded by the bill: every byte through the hub is processed.

notes.title: VPC Endpoints & PrivateLink — A Free Route, or an ENI with DNS
notes.html:
References

AWS: Gateway endpoints · AWS whitepaper: AWS PrivateLink · AWS: PrivateLink cross-region connectivity for AWS services · AWS: PrivateLink pricing

TL;DR

Endpoints let private workloads reach a service without the internet or a NAT gateway. There are two mechanisms:

  • Gateway endpoint (S3 and DynamoDB only): a prefix-list row in your route tables. It's free, and it removes NAT charges for that traffic.
  • Interface endpoint: an ENI with a private IP in each chosen AZ, plus private DNS that makes the service's normal name resolve to it. It's billed per AZ-hour and per GB.

PrivateLink is the interface mechanism pointed at your service behind an NLB. Consumers reach that one service, one way, with no routing into your VPC, even when the CIDRs overlap.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:app resolves sqs.ap-south-1.amazonaws.comprivate DNS answers the endpoint ENI's IPSG on the endpointendpoint policyservicenever touches NAT or the internet

Recall

Prompt Answer
Gateway vs interface endpoint, in one line each? Gateway: a free route-table prefix list for S3 or DynamoDB. Interface: a billed ENI per AZ plus DNS override.
Why does a peered VPC fail to use your S3 gateway endpoint? Gateway endpoints aren't transitive: only the VPC that owns the route can use them.
What does PrivateLink expose, compared with peering? One service behind an NLB, consumer → provider only; peering exposes whole CIDRs both ways.

The idea

An account's biggest network line item turns out to be NAT gateway processing. Almost all of it is the nightly 2 TB export to S3. S3 resolves to public addresses, so without an endpoint those bytes take the full NAT path, and none of that shows on the architecture diagram. One free gateway endpoint, a single route-table row, removes the charge.

The trade: endpoints keep traffic private and off NAT, and you pay nothing for the two gateway kinds and an hourly fee per AZ for every interface endpoint in every VPC, which adds up across an estate.

How it works

Which endpoint, from the destination.

Gateway endpoint Interface endpoint PrivateLink endpoint service
Mechanism prefix list in route tables ENI per AZ + private DNS your NLB (or GWLB) shared to consumers
Covers S3, DynamoDB most AWS services, partner services one service you publish
Cost free per AZ-hour + per GB consumer pays the interface endpoint; you pay the NLB
Reachable from peered VPC, VPN, on-prem no yes, by IP or forwarded DNS yes
Policy endpoint policy (IAM-style) endpoint policy + SG on the ENI allow-listed principals, acceptance
CIDR overlap n/a n/a fine: no routing between VPCs

Evolution

Lineage:May 2015 S3 gateway endpointNov 2017 PrivateLink, interface endpointsNov 2024 cross-region PrivateLink for endpoint servicesNov 2025 cross-region PrivateLink for AWS services
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: an interface endpoint can now reach a service in another region, gated by vpce:AllowMultiRegion; Route 53 Profiles can share endpoint private zones across many VPCs.
  • What won't change: gateway endpoints are a route, interface endpoints are DNS, and the failure modes follow from that.

On the wire

Terraform for both kinds, with the defaults that bite:

resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "s3" {
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  service_name      = "com.amazonaws.ap-south-1.s3"
  vpc_endpoint_type = "Gateway"                         # free; a route, not an ENI
  route_table_ids   = values(aws_route_table.private)[*].id   # forget one table and that
}                                                       # subnet still pays NAT for S3

resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "sqs" {
  vpc_id              = aws_vpc.main.id
  service_name        = "com.amazonaws.ap-south-1.sqs"
  vpc_endpoint_type   = "Interface"
  private_dns_enabled = true      # Terraform's default is FALSE: without it, SDKs keep
                                  # resolving the public name and go through NAT anyway
  subnet_ids          = values(aws_subnet.private)[*].id   # one ENI, one hourly charge, per AZ
  security_group_ids  = [aws_security_group.endpoints.id]  # must allow 443 from the clients
}

Measure it

  • See it: dig +short sqs.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com from an instance returns a 10.x address when private DNS works, public IPs when it doesn't; the route table shows a pl-… row for S3.
  • In production: NAT BytesOutToDestination falling after the endpoint; endpoint BytesProcessed; endpoint count × AZs as an hourly line.
  • Bounded by: interface-endpoint sprawl across VPCs → a central endpoint VPC behind the hub with shared private zones (private DNS).

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A gateway endpoint is a free route-table entry for S3 and DynamoDB, so that traffic stops paying NAT. An interface endpoint is an ENI in each AZ plus private DNS that redirects the service's normal name, billed per hour and GB. PrivateLink is the same mechanism for your own service behind an NLB: consumers reach one service, one way, and overlapping CIDRs don't matter.

Q · Mechanism — Why does an interface endpoint "just work" for existing code? Private DNS creates a hidden private zone for the service's public hostname in your VPC, answering with the endpoint ENIs' private IPs. SDKs keep using the same URL; resolution changes. That's also why it needs the VPC's DNS settings on and why on-prem clients need resolver forwarding.

Q · Trade-off — Interface endpoints in every VPC or centralised? Per VPC is simple and keeps traffic local, but costs AZs × services × VPCs in hourly fees. Central endpoints behind a Transit Gateway with shared private zones cut that to one set, paying TGW per-GB instead. Centralise when the count runs to hundreds; keep high-volume ones local.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Gateway endpoint cost free S3 and DynamoDB only default (as of Nov 2026): AWS PrivateLink pricing
Interface endpoint billing per AZ-hour + per GB one ENI per chosen AZ default (as of Nov 2026): AWS PrivateLink pricing
Model: nightly S3 export through NAT 2 TB/night of NAT-processed bytes all removable by one route illustrative

Pitfalls

  • "S3 traffic stays inside AWS anyway, so the endpoint is only security"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: S3 and your VPC are both "in AWS".
    ↳ Why it's wrong: S3 resolves to public IPs, so without a gateway endpoint it goes through NAT and is billed per GB processed.
    ↳ Think instead: a gateway endpoint is a cost fix first.
  • Not the same: gateway vs interface endpoint
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "VPC endpoints" on the same console page, and S3 offers both.
    ↳ Difference: gateway = route, free, VPC-local; interface = ENI with DNS, billed, reachable from peers and on-prem.
    ↳ Think instead: in-VPC S3 → gateway; on-prem S3 → interface.
  • Don't create an interface endpoint without private DNS.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: Terraform's default leaves it off and creation succeeds.
    ↳ What goes wrong: clients still resolve the public name and use NAT; you pay for the endpoint and the NAT.
    ↳ Do instead: private_dns_enabled = true and check with dig.
  • "PrivateLink needs non-overlapping CIDRs like peering"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it also connects two VPCs privately.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the consumer gets an ENI in its own VPC; nothing routes between the CIDRs.
    ↳ Think instead: PrivateLink is the answer when CIDRs overlap, for exposing a service.
  • Shelf life: route vs DNS mechanics are durable; cross-region support, service lists and prices change.

Connections

Path:IGW, NAT and egressendpoints and PrivateLinkprivate DNSthe bill
  • Builds on route tables (gateway) and private DNS (interface).
  • Owned elsewhere: cloud LBs own the NLB behind a PrivateLink service.
  • Breaks when combined with a peered VPC expecting your gateway endpoint: not transitive.
  • Bounded by posture: endpoint policies limit which buckets can be reached.

notes.title: Cloud Load Balancer Types — ALB, NLB, GWLB and Their GCP and Azure Twins
notes.html:
References

AWS: Application Load Balancers · AWS: Network Load Balancers · AWS: QUIC support for Network Load Balancer · Microsoft Learn: Azure Application Gateway

TL;DR

Every cloud splits its balancers by layer, and the L4 vs L7 table explains why. This note is the product map and its defaults:

  • ALB: L7. It terminates TLS, routes on host and path, balances per request, and plugs into WAF and OIDC.
  • NLB: L4, covering TCP, UDP, TLS and, since Nov 2025, QUIC passthrough. It holds a static IP per AZ and can keep the client's source IP.
  • GWLB: forwards whole packets to firewall appliances over GENEVE.
  • CLB: legacy, so don't use it.

The defaults that bite are idle timeouts, cross-zone settings and whether the client IP survives.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:DNS nameLB node in each enabled AZlistener (port, protocol)ruletarget grouphealthy targetcross-zone or same-zone

Recall

Prompt Answer
A partner must allow-list a fixed IP for your HTTP API that needs path routing. What do you deploy? NLB with Elastic IPs in front, an ALB registered as its target.
Default idle timeouts? ALB 60 s; NLB TCP 350 s, UDP 120 s (as of Nov 2026).
Cross-zone load balancing default? ALB on, no charge; NLB and GWLB off, and turning it on bills cross-AZ bytes.

The idea

A team moves a WebSocket service from ALB to NLB for a static IP. Connections that sat quiet for a minute used to drop at the ALB's 60 s timer. Now they survive until 350 s, and then die with a reset that no log explains. The NLB timer is longer but works differently: it drops the flow silently and resets the next packet.
