The trade: picking a cloud balancer picks a layer, and with it a set of defaults (timeouts, client IP, cross-zone) that matter more day to day than the throughput numbers on the product page.

How it works

The decision in three questions; the theory lives in L4 vs L7.

AWS ALB AWS NLB GCP Azure
L7 ALB — Application LB (global or regional) Application Gateway (regional), Front Door (global)
L4 — NLB Network LB (passthrough or proxy) Load Balancer
Static IP no, DNS name only yes, one per AZ, EIP optional anycast IP on global LBs yes
Client IP at target X-Forwarded-For preserved for instance targets; IP targets need it enabled or PROXY v2 header at L7, preserved at L4 passthrough header at L7, preserved at L4
Idle timeout default 60 s (1–4,000) TCP 350 s (60–6,000), UDP 120 s per product per product
Security groups yes yes, since Aug 2023 (only at creation) firewall rules NSGs

Evolution

Lineage:2009 Classic Load BalancerAug 2016 ALBSep 2017 NLBNov 2020 GWLBAug 2023 security groups on NLBNov 2025 NLB QUIC passthrough
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: QUIC passthrough keeps sessions sticky by QUIC connection ID across client IP changes; NLB security groups must be attached at creation or never.
  • What won't change: the L4/L7 split, so the capability sets stay disjoint.

On the wire

Terraform for NLB in front of ALB, with the defaults that bite:

resource "aws_lb" "edge" {
  load_balancer_type               = "network"
  enable_cross_zone_load_balancing = false   # NLB default false: uneven targets per AZ get uneven load
  security_groups                  = [aws_security_group.nlb.id]  # only settable at creation
  subnet_mapping {
    subnet_id     = aws_subnet.public["ap-south-1a"].id
    allocation_id = aws_eip.edge_a.id        # the IP the partner allow-lists
  }
}

resource "aws_lb_target_group" "alb" {
  target_type = "alb"                        # NLB forwards to the ALB, which does path routing
  protocol    = "TCP"
  port        = 443
}

resource "aws_lb" "app" {
  load_balancer_type = "application"
  idle_timeout       = 60                    # default; long-polls and WebSockets need keepalives under it
}

Measure it

  • See it: dig +short <alb-dns> returns changing IPs over time, an NLB's stay fixed; curl -sv to an ALB shows its headers, to an NLB the target's.
  • In production: ALB TargetResponseTime, HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count; NLB TCP_ELB_Reset_Count, UnHealthyHostCount per AZ; cross-zone bytes on the bill.
  • Bounded by: the idle timer → keepalives shorter than it (keepalives); lost client IP → preserve_client_ip or PROXY v2.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: AWS sells three balancers by layer. The ALB works at L7 for HTTP with path routing, WAF and auth. The NLB works at L4 for TCP, UDP and QUIC with a static IP and the client's address. The GWLB sends raw packets to firewall appliances. GCP and Azure make the same split under other names. I pick by what the balancer must see, then check the idle timeout and cross-zone defaults.

Q · Mechanism — Why can the NLB give a static IP and the ALB can't? An NLB has one node per AZ with a fixed address in that subnet, optionally an Elastic IP. An ALB is a fleet of proxies that scales by adding and replacing nodes, so it publishes a DNS name whose addresses change. For a fixed IP with L7 features, put an NLB in front of the ALB, or use Global Accelerator.

Q · Trade-off — Turn NLB cross-zone on? On spreads load evenly when AZs have different target counts, but every cross-AZ byte bills and a sick AZ's clients reach healthy targets elsewhere. Off keeps traffic and cost in-zone but skews load when targets are uneven. Default off is right with equal targets per AZ.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
ALB idle timeout 60 s, settable 1–4,000 s then the ALB closes the connection default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ALB docs
NLB idle timeout TCP 350 s (60–6,000), UDP 120 s then RST on the next packet default (as of Nov 2026): AWS NLB docs
GWLB encapsulation GENEVE, UDP 6081 appliance must speak GENEVE spec (as of Nov 2026): AWS GWLB docs

Pitfalls

  • "ALB and NLB are the same product at two prices"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: both are "Elastic Load Balancing" with similar consoles.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: they work at different layers; an NLB can't route by path or retry, an ALB can't hold a static IP or carry UDP.
    ↳ Think instead: pick the layer, then the product.
  • Don't raise the NLB idle timeout to keep quiet connections.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the setting goes to 6,000 s.
    ↳ What goes wrong: above 350 s the target's ENI connection tracking must match too, or flows die anyway.
    ↳ Do instead: keepalives shorter than 350 s.
  • Not the same: cross-zone on ALB vs on NLB
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: same setting name on the same service.
    ↳ Difference: ALB: on by default, no charge; NLB: off by default, cross-AZ bytes bill when on.
    ↳ Think instead: check the default per type, and the bill before enabling.
  • "Security groups can be added to an NLB later"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: ALBs and instances take SG changes at any time.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: an NLB created without SGs can never get them; you'd replace it, and its IPs.
    ↳ Think instead: attach an SG at creation, even a permissive one.
  • Shelf life: the layer split is durable; timeouts, QUIC, SG support and product names move.

Connections

Path:L4 vs L7cloud LB typesPrivateLinkingress, gateway, mesh
  • Builds on L4 load balancing: flow hashing and the client IP.
  • Owned elsewhere: health checks own check depth.
  • Breaks when combined with gRPC behind an NLB: one connection pins to one target.
  • Bounded by the bill: cross-zone bytes and LCUs.

notes.title: Private DNS in the Cloud — The .2 Resolver, Private Zones and Resolver Endpoints
notes.html:
References

AWS: Working with private hosted zones · AWS: Resolving DNS queries between VPCs and your network · AWS: Route 53 Profiles · AWS: Amazon DNS server

TL;DR

Every VPC has a resolver at its CIDR base + 2 (and 169.254.169.253). It answers in a fixed order:

  1. Private hosted zones associated with the VPC.
  2. AWS service names, including the zones that interface endpoints add.
  3. Forwarding rules to other resolvers.
  4. Public recursion.

A private zone is ordinary DNS made visible only to the VPCs you associate it with, which is how split-horizon works. A private zone owns its whole namespace inside the VPC: a name it doesn't hold gets NXDOMAIN, not a public answer. Resolver endpoints carry queries across the boundary: inbound, so on-prem can resolve cloud names, and outbound, so the VPC can forward to corporate DNS.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:app asks 10.20.0.2matching private zone? answer or NXDOMAINforwarding rule? to an outbound endpointelse recursive to public DNScached per TTL

Recall

Prompt Answer
Private zone example.com lacks www; public DNS has it. What does a VPC client get? NXDOMAIN: the private zone answers for the whole namespace.
Inbound vs outbound resolver endpoint? Inbound: on-prem queries cloud names through ENIs in your VPC. Outbound: the VPC forwards matching names to on-prem DNS.
Which VPC settings must be on for private zones? enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames.

The idea

A team creates a private hosted zone example.com so that api.example.com resolves to an internal load balancer from inside the VPC. That afternoon, every job that calls www.example.com or auth.example.com fails with NXDOMAIN, but only from inside the VPC. A laptop resolves both fine.

Nothing is broken. The private zone matched first and answered for everything under example.com, including the names it doesn't hold.

The trade: private zones give you split-horizon names without running DNS servers, and you pay with a zone that shadows the public one for its entire subtree inside the VPC.

How it works

Who answers a query from inside the VPC, in order.

Piece Answers Scope Cost shape
VPC resolver (base + 2) everything, as the entry point one VPC, 1,024 packets/s per ENI free
Private hosted zone names you define VPCs you associate, cross-account allowed per zone + per query
Interface endpoint private DNS the AWS service's public name the endpoint's VPC part of the endpoint
Inbound / outbound endpoint cloud names for on-prem / on-prem names for the cloud region; rules shareable via RAM per ENI-hour + per query
Route 53 Profile a bundle of zones, rules and DNS Firewall many VPCs and accounts per profile association

When a forwarding rule and a private zone match the same name, the more specific domain wins; for equal names, the rule wins.

Evolution

Lineage:2014 Route 53 private hosted zonesNov 2018 Resolver endpoints and rulesMar 2021 Resolver DNS FirewallApr 2024 Route 53 ProfilesApr 2025 Profiles share interface-endpoint zones
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: Profiles replaced per-VPC association scripts in multi-account estates.
  • What won't change: the namespace-ownership rule, which is ordinary DNS authority (DNS resolution).

On the wire

Terraform for split-horizon without shadowing, with the defaults that bite:

resource "aws_route53_zone" "internal" {
  name = "internal.example.com"     # a SUBDOMAIN, not example.com: nothing public is shadowed
  vpc { vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id }  # associated VPCs only; an unassociated VPC gets public DNS
}

resource "aws_route53_resolver_rule" "corp" {
  domain_name          = "corp.example.net"
  rule_type            = "FORWARD"
  resolver_endpoint_id = aws_route53_resolver_endpoint.outbound.id
  target_ip { ip = "192.168.10.53" }  # on-prem DNS, reached over VPN or Direct Connect
}                                     # the rule does nothing until associated with each VPC

Measure it

  • See it: dig api.internal.example.com @10.20.0.2 from an instance; dig www.example.com @10.20.0.2 vs @1.1.1.1 exposes shadowing; Resolver query logs show which rule answered.
  • In production: NXDOMAIN rate from Resolver query logs; resolver endpoint ENI query counts; ethtool -S linklocal_allowance_exceeded when an instance passes 1,024 DNS packets/s.
  • Bounded by: the per-ENI packet limit → a local caching resolver (e.g. systemd-resolved, NodeLocal DNSCache); shadowing → subdomain zones.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Each VPC's resolver at base + 2 answers private hosted zones first, then forwarding rules, then public recursion. A private zone is visible only to associated VPCs, which gives split-horizon, and it owns its whole subtree, so a missing record is NXDOMAIN, not a public fallback. Resolver endpoints bridge to on-prem: inbound for on-prem asking cloud names, outbound with rules for the reverse.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a missing private record not fall through to public DNS? The resolver treats the private zone as authoritative for that domain. Authority means "the answer is here, including that the name doesn't exist". Falling through would make results depend on which zone happened to lack a record, so DNS never does it.

Q · Trade-off — Private zone named example.com or internal.example.com? A subdomain. Mirroring the public zone gives one set of names inside and out, but every public record must be copied into the private zone or it vanishes inside the VPC. A dedicated subdomain shadows nothing.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Resolver addresses base + 2, 169.254.169.253 fd00:ec2::253 for IPv6 on Nitro spec (as of Nov 2026): AWS Amazon DNS docs
Packets to the Amazon resolver 1,024 per second per ENI drops beyond it, silently default (as of Nov 2026): AWS Amazon DNS docs

Pitfalls

  • "A missing private record falls through to public DNS"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it feels like an overlay on top of public DNS.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the private zone is authoritative for its whole namespace inside the VPC, so missing means NXDOMAIN.
    ↳ Think instead: use a subdomain zone, or copy every public record.
  • "A private zone is private because it holds internal IPs"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: that's what people put in them.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: privacy is the VPC association; the records can be anything, public IPs included.
    ↳ Think instead: who is associated decides who sees it.
  • Not the same: inbound vs outbound resolver endpoint
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the names describe direction, but from whose side?
    ↳ Difference: inbound accepts queries into AWS from on-prem; outbound sends queries out to on-prem per a rule.
    ↳ Think instead: name the direction of the query, not of the traffic.
  • Don't point every pod at the VPC resolver directly at scale.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the default and it works in testing.
    ↳ What goes wrong: busy nodes pass 1,024 packets/s per ENI and lookups drop, which looks like flaky upstreams.
    ↳ Do instead: a node-local cache, which CoreDNS covers.
  • Shelf life: authority and split-horizon are durable; Profiles, Firewall and limits evolve.

Connections

Path:private DNS and service discoveryprivate DNS in the cloudendpointsmulti-region
  • Builds on TTL and caching layers: every answer here is cached by someone.
  • Owned elsewhere: DNS resolution owns recursion and authority.
  • Breaks when combined with DNS as an outage cause: one resolver limit, every service down.
  • Bounded by the VPC's DNS settings: off means no resolver at all.

notes.title: Data Transfer Cost — Every Boundary Is a Meter, and Meters Stack
notes.html:
References

AWS: Overview of data transfer costs for common architectures · AWS: Understanding data transfer costs for container services · AWS: NAT gateway pricing · Kubernetes: Topology aware routing

TL;DR

Traffic between private addresses in one AZ is free. Everything else is metered per GB: the AZ line (charged on both sides), a NAT gateway, a Transit Gateway, an interface endpoint, the region line and the internet. The meters stack. One GB from a private subnet to a vendor API, through a hub and a NAT gateway in another AZ, is charged five times. The fixes are ranked by arithmetic: remove a meter (a free gateway endpoint, NAT per AZ, zone-aware routing), then keep traffic local, and only then shrink bytes.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:byte leaves the ENIcrosses an AZ? meter ×2through TGW? meterthrough NAT? meterleaves the region or to the internet? meterthe bill, by usage type

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which traffic is free? Same AZ, private IPs, and gateway endpoints to S3 and DynamoDB.
Zone-blind Service in a 3-AZ cluster: share of calls crossing AZs? Two thirds, (n−1)/n, each billed on both sides.
The highest-return fix, usually? An S3 gateway endpoint: free, one route, removes NAT processing.

The idea

A team spreads a microservice fleet across three AZs for resilience and turns on a single shared NAT gateway to save on hourly fees. The next month the data-transfer line is larger than the compute line. Nothing on the diagram changed. Two thirds of internal calls cross a zone, every egress byte from two of the three zones crosses to the NAT, and each of those crossings is billed twice.

The trade: multi-AZ buys survival of a zone failure, and you pay per GB for every internal byte that crosses a zone line, a bill the architecture diagram never shows.

How it works

The trace, 1 GB at a time; counts are meters, not prices (from the model below).

Path for 1 GB Meters hit Meters Removed by
Same AZ, private IP none 0 —
Call to a pod in another AZ cross-AZ out + in 2 topology-aware routing
S3 via NAT in another AZ cross-AZ ×2 + NAT processing 3 S3 gateway endpoint → 0
Vendor API via hub + NAT in another AZ TGW + cross-AZ ×2 + NAT + internet 5 local NAT per AZ → 2
Cross-region replication inter-region transfer 1+ replicate once, read locally 
share of calls crossing AZs (zone-blind)  = (n − 1) / n        ← 2 AZs: 1/2 · 3 AZs: 2/3
billed cross-AZ GB                        = GB × (n − 1)/n × 2  ← both sides of the line
NAT per AZ pays off when                  = cross-AZ GB saved × rate > extra gateway-hours

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): the meter layout has held for a decade; rates move.
  • Changed recently: Kubernetes trafficDistribution (field GA in 1.33; PreferSameZone, which replaced PreferClose, stable in 1.35) made zone-local routing a one-line Service setting.
  • What won't change: a boundary that costs the provider bandwidth gets a meter.

On the wire

The command that finds the meters: the bill grouped by usage type.

aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-11-01 \
  --granularity MONTHLY --metrics UnblendedCost UsageQuantity \
  --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=USAGE_TYPE \
  --filter '{"Dimensions":{"Key":"USAGE_TYPE_GROUP","Values":["EC2: Data Transfer - Inter AZ","EC2: NAT Gateway - Data Processed","EC2: Data Transfer - Internet (Out)"]}}'
# look for: APS3-DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes (cross-AZ), APS3-NatGateway-Bytes (NAT), …-Out-Bytes (internet)
# the default that bites: a Service with no trafficDistribution spreads calls across all zones

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): meters per path and the zone-blind share.

cross = sum(random.randrange(3) != random.randrange(3) for _ in range(200_000))
gb = 20_000_000 * 12 * 50_000 / 1e9      # 20M requests × 12 internal calls × 50 KB
print(cross / 200_000, gb, gb * 2/3 * 2)
# look for: the crossing share, and billed GB above total internal GB
# naive belief predicts: "internal traffic is free"; at most 1/3 crosses

Run: 0.665 of calls crossed (exact 2/3). 12,000 internal GB a month became 16,000 billed cross-AZ GB, more than the traffic itself, because both sides pay.

Measure it

  • See it: Cost Explorer by usage type: DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes, NatGateway-Bytes, DataTransfer-Out-Bytes; VPC flow logs with az-id fields show which pairs cross.
  • In production: data transfer as a share of the bill, tracked monthly; NAT BytesOutToDestination per gateway; top talkers by flow logs.
  • Bounded by: resilience: keeping traffic in one AZ beyond routing preference reintroduces the single-zone outage (AZ planning).

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Inside one AZ on private IPs it's free; every boundary after that is a per-GB meter: cross-AZ on both sides, NAT, Transit Gateway, interface endpoints, inter-region and internet. They stack, so one GB can be billed five times. I remove meters first, with gateway endpoints, NAT per AZ and zone-aware routing, then localise, then compress.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a Kubernetes cluster pay so much cross-AZ? A Service picks among all ready endpoints regardless of zone, so with three zones two thirds of calls leave the caller's zone, and both sides are billed. A request that fans out to a dozen internal calls multiplies that, and none of it appears at the perimeter. trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone keeps calls in-zone when local endpoints exist.

Q · Trade-off — One shared NAT gateway or one per AZ? One shared NAT saves two hourly charges but sends egress from two of three zones across the AZ line, billed twice, and makes one zone a dependency for all internet access. Per AZ costs more hours and removes both problems. Above a modest egress volume, per AZ is cheaper as well as safer; compute it from your own NAT GB.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Zone-blind crossing share (n−1)/n: 1/2, 2/3 2 and 3 AZs derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Meters on the worst common path 5 hub + remote NAT + internet derived from the trace
Model: fan-out fleet, 3 AZs 12,000 GB → 16,000 GB billed 20M req × 12 calls × 50 KB illustrative
Cross-AZ direction charged on both sides per GB each way default (as of Nov 2026): AWS data transfer pricing

Pitfalls

  • "Traffic inside a VPC is free"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's all private addresses on one network.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: only same-AZ traffic is free; crossing a zone is billed per GB on both sides, and multi-AZ fleets cross constantly.
    ↳ Think instead: free means same AZ, not same VPC.
  • "One NAT gateway is the cheap option"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the hourly line is the visible one.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it adds cross-AZ transfer on most egress plus a single-zone dependency; past modest volume it costs more.
    ↳ Think instead: compute NAT GB × cross-AZ rate against two gateway-hours.
  • Don't compress before removing meters.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: compression is code you control and feels like engineering.
    ↳ What goes wrong: it trims a share of one meter, while a free endpoint removes whole meters at once.
    ↳ Do instead: remove, localise, then shrink, in that order.
  • Not the same: centralised egress vs cheaper egress
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are sold as "fewer NAT gateways".
    ↳ Difference: a hub removes hourly charges and adds per-GB TGW processing; for heavy VPCs that's a net loss.
    ↳ Think instead: central for control, local for volume.
  • Shelf life: the meter layout is durable; rates, usage-type names and Kubernetes routing settings move.

Connections

Path:IGW, NAT and egressthe billmulti-regionposture
  • Builds on endpoints: the gateway endpoint is the biggest single fix.
  • Owned elsewhere: Transit Gateway owns hub processing; cloud LBs own cross-zone balancing.
  • Breaks when combined with zone-blind service routing in Kubernetes Services.
  • Bounded by availability: single-AZ placement trades the bill for an outage.

notes.title: Multi-Region Networking — Routing Is Easy, the Data Is the Project
notes.html:
References

AWS: Route 53 failover routing · AWS: Latency-based routing · AWS: Global Accelerator · AWS whitepaper: Disaster recovery of workloads

TL;DR

Multi-region is three problems that get discussed as one:

  • Routing: sending a user to a region. It's solved by latency or failover DNS, or by anycast through Global Accelerator.
  • Latency: 70–250 ms between regions, paid per call. So nothing on the request path may call another region synchronously.
  • Data: the actual project. Active-passive means one writer, a non-zero RPO and a failover you must rehearse. Active-active means conflicts, unless each record has one home region.

The network is the easy third.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:userDNS (latency or failover) or anycast IPnearest healthy regionregion-local app, cache, readswrites to the home regionasync replication to the others

Recall

Prompt Answer
Eight sequential calls to a region 150 ms away cost? 1.2 s of network time before any work.
What does failover time add up to? Detection (interval × threshold) + TTL + caches ignoring it + DB promotion.
Active-active without conflict work: how? Partition by home region, so every record has one writer.

The idea

A team "goes multi-region" by deploying the app in a second region behind latency-based DNS, leaving the database in the first. Users near the new region now get slower pages: every query crosses 150 ms of ocean. When the first region fails, the second fails with it, because its database is gone. They built one region with a remote frontend.

The trade: a second region buys survival of a regional outage and lower latency for distant users, and you pay with a data-layer design (replication, consistency, failover) that the network can't do for you.

How it works

Active-passive with one writer; the dashed line is the only cross-region dependency.

Active-passive Active-active, partitioned Active-active, shared writes
Writers per record one region one (the home region) any region
RPO > 0: in-flight writes lost > 0 for the failed partition ≈ 0, with conflicts
Failover detect + DNS + promote re-home the failed partition none
Cross-region traffic replication only replication + some reads continuous, both ways
Cost of the choice an idle or unproven standby a partition key everywhere conflict resolution, forever 
network time  = sequential cross-region calls × RTT    ← 8 × 150 ms = 1.2 s
failover time = interval × threshold + TTL + promote   ← 30×3 + 60 + 60 = 210 s, then stale caches

Evolution

Lineage:2013 Route 53 failover and latency routingNov 2018 Global Accelerator (anycast, no DNS caching)Jul 2022 Cloud WANNov 2023 Route 53 Application Recovery Controller zonal shift2025 ARC Region switch
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: Application Recovery Controller adds rehearsed, runbook-driven region switches on top of DNS.
  • What won't change: the speed of light in fibre sets the RTT; no product lowers it.

On the wire

Terraform for DNS failover, with the default that bites:

resource "aws_route53_health_check" "a" {
  fqdn              = "a.api.example.com"
  type              = "HTTPS"
  resource_path     = "/healthz/deep"   # a shallow check passes while the DB is down
  request_interval  = 30                # default 30 s; 10 s costs more and detects faster
  failure_threshold = 3                 # default 3: 90 s to detect, before any TTL
}

resource "aws_route53_record" "primary" {
  name            = "api.example.com"
  type            = "A"
  set_identifier  = "a"
  health_check_id = aws_route53_health_check.a.id
  failover_routing_policy { type = "PRIMARY" }
  alias {
    name                   = aws_lb.a.dns_name
    zone_id                = aws_lb.a.zone_id
    evaluate_target_health = true       # Terraform has no default: false means an empty target
  }                                     # group still counts as healthy
}

Measure it

  • See it: dig api.example.com from two continents shows which region answers; a game day that fails region A, timed from first error to 95% of traffic in B.
  • In production: replication lag in seconds (that's the RPO); cross-region RTT per region pair; inter-region GB on the bill.
  • Bounded by: DNS caching → anycast global load balancing; residency rules → where data may be stored and processed.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Multi-region is routing, latency and data. Routing is latency or failover DNS, or anycast. Latency rules out synchronous cross-region calls on a request path. Data is the real work: active-passive gives one writer and a rehearsed failover with RPO above zero; active-active is safe only if each record has a home region. I exhaust multi-AZ first.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a 60-second TTL not give 60-second failover? Failover is a sum: health checks need interval × threshold to declare failure, then the TTL runs, then resolvers and clients that ignore TTLs keep the old answer, then the database replica is promoted. With defaults that's about 210 s before the long tail of cached clients. Anycast avoids the DNS terms.

Q · Trade-off — Active-active or active-passive? Active-passive keeps one writer and simple consistency, at the price of lost in-flight writes and a standby that's only proven if you rehearse it. Active-active removes failover and serves users locally, but shared writes need a conflict model. Default to active-passive with scheduled drills; go active-active when users partition by home region.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Inter-region RTT ~70–250 ms nearby to antipodal pairs measured (as of Nov 2026): typical published inter-region latency
Route 53 health check 30 s interval, threshold 3 10 s interval optional default (as of Nov 2026): Route 53 docs
Model: detection + TTL + promotion 210 s 30 × 3 + 60 + 60 derived; model run 24 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "Multi-region is mostly a networking problem"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: DNS routing and inter-region links are the visible pieces.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: they take days; replication, consistency and failover in the data layer take the months.
    ↳ Think instead: design the data path first, then route to it.
  • Don't split compute across regions while data stays in one.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it looks like a cheap first step.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every query pays the cross-region RTT and the second region still dies with the first.
    ↳ Do instead: move data and compute together, or don't move.
  • "Lowering the TTL makes failover fast"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the TTL is the number on the record.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: detection and promotion are usually larger, and many clients ignore TTLs.
    ↳ Think instead: time the whole sum in a drill, and use anycast for tight targets.
  • Not the same: multi-AZ vs multi-region
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "redundancy" with a failover story.
    ↳ Difference: multi-AZ is single-digit ms apart with synchronous replication; multi-region is 70–250 ms with async replication and an RPO.
    ↳ Think instead: multi-AZ for the common failure, multi-region for the rare one.
  • Shelf life: the routing/latency/data split is durable; ARC features and health-check options move.

Connections

Path:Transit Gatewaymulti-regionglobal load balancingcascading failures
  • Builds on DNS load balancing and TTL and caching layers.
  • Owned elsewhere: global load balancing owns anycast and GSLB; health checks own check depth.
  • Breaks when combined with synchronous cross-region calls in timeout budgets.
  • Bounded by the bill: replication is inter-region GB, continuously.

notes.title: Network Security Posture — Private by Route, Egress by Hostname, IMDSv2 Always
notes.html:
References

AWS: Configure the instance metadata service · AWS: Block public access to VPCs and subnets · AWS Network Firewall: domain filtering · AWS: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall

TL;DR

A cloud network posture is four decisions you make once and enforce everywhere:

  • Private by route: no workload subnet has a route to an internet gateway unless something must be reachable. VPC Block Public Access enforces this at account level.
  • Egress by hostname: outbound is an allow-list of names, enforced where the name is visible (a proxy, SNI filtering, DNS Firewall), because NAT only sees addresses.
  • IMDSv2 only: the metadata service at 169.254.169.254 hands out credentials, and the v2 token plus hop limit 1 is what stops SSRF and containers from taking them.
  • Identity over location: SG references and service identity, not CIDR trust.
Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:attacker finds SSRFasks 169.254.169.254 for credentialsIMDSv2 demands a PUT token, so it failstries to exfiltrateegress allow-list drops an unknown hostflow log and DNS Firewall alert

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does IMDSv2 add? A PUT session token with a TTL; hop limit 1 stops it leaving the host.
Why can't NAT enforce an egress allow-list? NAT sees IPs; the hostname lives in DNS, SNI or the Host header.
What does VPC Block Public Access do? Blocks IGW traffic for whole VPCs or accounts, overriding route tables.

The idea

A web app has an SSRF bug: it fetches any URL a user supplies. With IMDSv1, one request to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/app-role returns live role credentials. The attacker then uses them from home, because nothing limits where the role's keys work and nothing limits where the instance can send data.

The same bug against IMDSv2 returns 401. An SSRF can forge a GET, but it can't do the PUT handshake with a custom header first.

The trade: a strict posture closes whole classes of breach at the network layer, and you pay with friction: every new outbound dependency is a change request, and every legacy agent must speak IMDSv2.

How it works

The breach path and the control that breaks each link.

On the wire

The IMDSv2 exchange from inside an instance, and the account-wide default:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
# 401   ← IMDSv2 required: a plain GET, as an SSRF would send, is refused
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token \
  -H 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 300')
curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-id
# i-0abc…   ← the PUT + header handshake works locally; the token TTL caps its life

aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-defaults --http-tokens required --http-put-response-hop-limit 1
# the default that bites: instances launched before this, or from old launch templates,
# keep "optional" (v1 allowed); containers needing IMDS want hop limit 2, and nothing else does

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Four decisions. Private by route: no IGW route for workloads, enforced by VPC Block Public Access. Egress by hostname through a proxy, SNI filtering or DNS Firewall, because NAT sees only IPs. IMDSv2 required with hop limit 1, which defeats SSRF credential theft. And identity over location: SG references and service identity rather than CIDR trust. Plus flow and DNS logs to see it.

Q · Mechanism — Why does IMDSv2 defeat SSRF? An SSRF bug lets an attacker make the server send a request, usually a GET to a chosen URL, rarely with custom methods and headers. IMDSv2 requires a PUT with a TTL header to get a token, then the token as a header on every read. Hop limit 1 means the token reply dies after one hop, so a container or a forwarded request can't use it.

Q · Trade-off — Hostname allow-list or open egress with monitoring? An allow-list stops exfiltration and command-and-control to unknown hosts outright, but every new SaaS dependency needs a change, and a slow process gets bypassed. Open egress with alerting costs nothing in friction and catches problems after the fact. Allow-list for production data paths; monitor-only for build and dev, with a fast approval path.

Pitfalls

  • "Private subnet means safe"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: nothing can connect in from the internet.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: most breaches start from inside (an SSRF, a dependency) and leave through open egress via NAT.
    ↳ Think instead: inbound and outbound are separate controls; private only covers inbound.
  • "Security groups can enforce an egress allow-list"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: SGs have outbound rules.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: they match IPs, and SaaS and CDN hosts share and rotate addresses.
    ↳ Think instead: names need a name-aware control: proxy, SNI or DNS Firewall.
  • Don't set hop limit 2 fleet-wide for one container use case.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it makes the containerised agent work everywhere.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every container on every host can now fetch the node's role credentials.
    ↳ Do instead: hop limit 1, and give pods their own identity (IRSA or EKS Pod Identity).
  • Not the same: DNS Firewall vs Network Firewall domain filtering
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both block by domain name.
    ↳ Difference: DNS Firewall blocks the lookup, which hard-coded IPs bypass; Network Firewall checks SNI or Host on the connection itself.
    ↳ Think instead: DNS for cheap breadth, SNI for enforcement.
  • Shelf life: the four decisions are durable; IMDS defaults, BPA modes and firewall features move.
